In this lesson, you will observe the operation of a typical PCM transmitter and receiver circuit.
INTRODUCTIONM
In the first part of the experiment, you will set up, align and observe the signals in the transmitter or modulator circuit.
In the second part of the experiment, you will set up, align and observe the signals in the receiver or demodulator circuit.
The circuits are typical, that is you may not find the exact circuits in commercial equipment.
However, the circuits operate as any PCM modulator and demodulator.
Once learned, you will have the knowledge and skill to operate and maintain any PCM system.
In this lesson you will observe the operation of PCM transmitters and receivers.

In this experiment, you will observe the operation and measure signals in a typical PCM transmitter circuit.
EXPERIMENT
The transmitter circuit is contained on PC130-326 and consists of five major sections.
The amplifier circuit is used to scale the analog input voltage.
The Analog to Digital Converter converts the analog information to digital.
The output of the A/D is also used to drive a display card,
The display card is used to give you a visual indication of the output of the A/D converter.
The Parallel to Serial Converter changes the parallel output of the A/D converter to serial.
The Output Multiplexer adds the sync pulse to the serial data. Then the entire frame is transmitted out.
The Timer/Sync Bit Generator generates the sync pulse and controls the operation of the A/D and P/S converters.
Now, pick up the PC130-326 card and compare to the schematic.
Notice R7, R10 and R14. These variable resistors are used to align the PCM modulator.
Also notice J1 on the card. This is the parallel output to the display card.

The decoders used in the circuit do not decode the binary numbers from 1010 to 1111 into hexadecimal letters, A through F.
Therefore, the seven segment displays will not be used in this experiment; however, they will show the numbers 0 through 9.

To determine if the A/D and S/P converters are operating correctly, you must calculate the binary output of the modulator for a given analog voltage input. This is where the quantization level and quantization level voltage spacing comes into play.
Knowing that the A/D converter produces an 8 bit output (ignore sync pulse for right now), calculate and type in the quantization level.
Remember, the quantization level equals two to the power and is 8 in this circuit.
TRY AGAIN!
QUANTIZATION LEVEL - The quantization level of an A/D converter is equal to two to the power where equals the number of bits in the converter.
You still have not calculated the correct quantization level. You should have calculated 256 because equals 8.
Knowing that q is 256, calculate and type in, rounded to three decimal places, the voltage between levels (remember, the maximum Vpp is 10).
Remember, the voltage spacing is the maximum input voltage divided by the quantization level minus 1. Recalculate the voltage spacing.
TRY AGAIN!
VOLTAGE SPACING - The voltage between levels in an A/D converter is equal to the maximum voltage input divided by the quantization level minus 1.
You still have not calculated the correct voltage spacing between quantization levels. You should have calculated 0.039 which is 10 divided by 255 and rounded off to three places.
Now, to determine the binary output of the A/D converter, you must determine the number of levels for a particular input voltage. Let's use a voltage of 7.5 volts.
Dividing 7.5 volts by the voltage level spacing produces 192.30. Since the quantization levels are always a whole number, the output level for a 7.5 volt input is 192 out of 256.
Changing the level of 191 into binary produces 10111111. 1011111 should be the output of the A/D converter for an input of 7.5 volts. Let's check.

In this experiment, you will observe the operation and measure signals in a typical PCM receiver circuit.
EXPERIMENT
The receiver circuit is contained on PC130-327 and consists of six major sections.
The input amplifier circuit is used to compensate for attenuation and distortion caused by the transmission medium.
The serial to parallel converter changes the serial input PCM data to parallel.
The digital to analog converter converts the parallel digital data to analog.
The Output Amplifier is used to filter and amplify the analog output signal.
The SYNC Bit Detector locates the SYNC pulse and initializes the timing circuit.
The timing section controls the serial to parallel conversion. The conversion only takes place after the eight data bits have been loaded.
Now, pick up the PC130-327 card and compare to the schematic.
Notice the five variable resistor, R4, R5, R6, R7 and R9.
R4, R5 and R6 set the SYNC bit detector, R7 sets the bandwidth and R9 calibrates the D/A converter.
Also, the output of the serial to parallel converter, IC2, connects to J1. J1 is used to connect a display.
Match up the other components on the card to the schematic.

In this experiment, you will observe the operation and measure signals in a typical PCM receiver circuit.
EXPERIMENT
The receiver circuit is contained on PC130-327 and consists of six major sections.
The input amplifier circuit is used to compensate for attenuation and distortion caused by the transmission medium.
The serial to parallel converter changes the serial input PCM data to parallel.
The digital to analog converter converts the parallel digital data to analog.
The Output Amplifier is used to filter and amplify the analog output signal.
The SYNC Bit Detector locates the SYNC pulse and initializes the timing circuit.
The timing section controls the serial to parallel conversion. The conversion only takes place after the eight data bits have been loaded.

R4, R5 and R6 set the SYNC bit detector, R7 sets the bandwidth and R9 calibrates the D/A converter.
Also, the output of the serial to parallel converter, IC2, connects to J1. J1 is used to connect a display.
